title: The Harvest of Vessel Farm
premise: Ines Ishikawa returns to Vessel Farm, the house her family abandoned twenty years ago, to appraise it for a probate sale — but the survey instruments register the property as larger inside than out, and her childhood imaginary friend, Marrow, is waiting on the porch exactly as she left him. The farm 'counts' its residents: every generation it harvests one family member on the autumn equinox, and this year the count falls due with Ines's estranged sister and nephew living in the house. As Ines documents the farm's ledger of past takings hidden in the walls, she discovers their grandmother bargained the family's names away to escape poverty — and that the debt can be paid only by someone who consents. Ines offers herself in her nephew's place, but at the moment of harvest she turns the count against the farm itself, entering herself into the ledger as its owner rather than its crop, and the house, which must obey its own records, lets the family go while collapsing inward around her.
about_author: Mirabel Dunmore spent a decade as a rural land assessor in the Pacific Northwest before turning to fiction, and her horror is shaped by the deeds, easements, and boundary disputes of that work. She writes from a farmhouse she has never fully finished surveying.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Ines arrives at Vessel Farm to appraise it for probate, armed with clipboards, laser measures, and a habit of documenting everything as a form of prayer. The interior rooms measure larger than the exterior footprint; her instruments disagree with themselves. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: professional composure cracking into unease as the numbers stop behaving.

chapters.title: Marrow
chapters.summary: On the porch sits Marrow, her childhood imaginary friend, unchanged after twenty years, greeting her by name. Her sister Dana and nephew Theo live in the house and have seen him too — Dana dismisses him, Theo plays with him. Ines finds fresh tally marks scratched inside a closet wall. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: dread braided with an awful, tender familiarity.

chapters.title: What the Walls Kept
chapters.summary: Tearing back lath during a structural inspection, Ines uncovers a ledger: generations of names, dates, and tallies, each entry ending with a single name struck through. The last dated entry is her grandmother's handwriting, and the next equinox line is blank except for Theo's initials, already begun. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: horror curdling into protective fury.

chapters.title: Dana's Denial
chapters.summary: Ines confronts Dana, who admits strange things — doors opening onto rooms they shouldn't, Theo counting aloud in his sleep — but refuses to leave; the farm is the only asset left and leaving means admitting their childhood exile was their mother's flight from something real. POV: Dana. Emotional beat: resentment and fear wearing the mask of practicality.

chapters.title: The Boundary Walk
chapters.summary: Ines surveys the property lines and finds the farm's boundaries move overnight, annexing a neighbor's field, and meets elderly Ruth Calloway next door, whose own family was harvested in 1968. Ruth explains the count: one per generation, taken at equinox, always the one who consents or the one who is chosen. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: the relief of being believed, shadowed by hopelessness.

chapters.title: Theo's Friend
chapters.summary: Theo tells Ines that Marrow has been teaching him a game called 'getting ready,' where he practices standing very still and saying yes. Ines realizes the farm is grooming its chosen heir and tries to sever Theo's connection, but Marrow appears to her directly, pleading that he only ever wanted to keep her safe — he was made by the farm, not by her. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: grief for the friend who was never hers.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Bargain
chapters.summary: In the county archive, Ines finds the 1974 deed: her grandmother signed away 'the issue of her issue' in exchange for the farm saving them from bankruptcy. The clause renews each generation unless a named owner revokes it — and the current owner of record is the estate, meaning whoever inherits can rewrite the terms. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: cold clarity; justice exists outside the law, but the law left a door open.

chapters.title: Equinox Eve
chapters.summary: Dana finally agrees to flee, but the roads loop back to the farm no matter which way they drive; the property has closed around them like a hand. They barricade in the kitchen while tally marks bloom across every wall, counting down hours. Marrow stands outside the window all night, weeping. POV: alternating Ines and Dana. Emotional beat: claustrophobic solidarity on the edge of surrender.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: At equinox dawn the house begins taking Theo, pulling him toward the cellar root-cellar door that wasn't there yesterday. Ines intervenes, declaring consent in his place, and follows the harvest down — but instead of offering herself as crop, she signs the ledger's blank ownership line with her own name, claiming the farm as its inheritor. The count, bound to obey its records, reverses. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into deliberate sacrifice and defiance.

chapters.title: Deed and Aftermath
chapters.summary: The farm collapses inward, rooms folding shut behind the fleeing family, and Ines walks out last as owner of a property that no longer exists on any map. Weeks later, Dana and Theo settle elsewhere; Ines keeps the burned ledger pages, documents everything still, and sometimes feels a small presence at the edge of new houses she surveys — patient, waiting to be claimed or refused. POV: Ines. Emotional beat: scarred peace, vigilance, and the question of what she now carries.
